etymology: Pictograph: a tall watchtower or gate-building — roof at the top, upper chamber, and the gateway below. 'High' in every later sense, including prices.
mnemonic: A pagoda drawn floor by floor: roof, window, gate — たかい. High building, high rank, high price: the tower charges admission.

etymology: Phono-semantic: movement (辶) + 周 'circuit, all around' (phonetic シュウ) — going one full round. Applied to the seven-day cycle when Japan adopted the Western week.
mnemonic: Walk one full lap (周) around the calendar and you're back where you started: one week — シュウ. 毎週, every lap.

etymology: Simplified from 學: a child (子) under a roof, with hands above passing knowledge down. The three little strokes on top are all that remain of those hands.
mnemonic: A child under a sparkling roof — sparks of knowledge raining down from the teacher's hands: to study, まなぶ. 学校 is where the sparks fly, ガッコウ.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a hand gripping a brush (聿) over a tablet (the 日-shaped block below) — the act of writing caught mid-stroke.
mnemonic: A hand pressing a brush down onto the page, line after line — かく. The stacked horizontals are the ruled lines of the notebook; 図書館 keeps what the brush leaves behind.

etymology: Pictograph: a mouth (口) with sound waves rising from it — speech leaving the lips. As a left-side component it marks nearly everything said in the language.
mnemonic: Four sound waves stacked over a mouth: words on their way out — いう. Whenever 言 stands at the left of a kanji, somebody is talking.

etymology: Phono-semantic: words (言) + tongue (舌, from an older phonetic) — the tongue shaping words into a story or conversation.
mnemonic: Words (言) rolled off a tongue (舌) and braided into a tale — はなし. Phone conversations are 電話: electric talk.

etymology: Phono-semantic: words (言) + 吾 'I, we' (phonetic ゴ) — speech exchanged between me and you: language.
mnemonic: My (吾) words (言) — the language I carry: ゴ. It closes the name of every tongue on earth: 日本語, フランス語, and yours next.

etymology: Phono-semantic: words (言) + 売 'sell' (simplified from 賣, the old phonetic ドク/トク) — words offered up like wares, taken in by reading.
mnemonic: A street seller (売) hawking words (言) aloud — and you, reading the signboard: よむ. 読書 is buying stories with your eyes.

etymology: Pictograph: the vault of the sky as a canopy, with four drops falling inside it. As a crown component it governs all weather kanji (雪, 雲, 電).
mnemonic: A window pane in a storm: four drops caught mid-fall behind the glass — あめ. When 雨 sits on a kanji's head, look up: weather incoming.

etymology: Ideograph: a line drawn above the big person (大) — that which stretches over every head: heaven, the sky.
mnemonic: The widest thing a person (大) can point at is the line above them: the heavens — てん. 天気 is the sky's mood today.

etymology: Pictograph: a person standing squarely on the ground line, arms out for balance — the act of standing itself.
mnemonic: Feet planted on the floor line, arms out: stand up! — たつ. A lamp standing at attention on its base; it holds this pose inside 駅 platforms and 立入禁止 signs alike.

etymology: Compound ideograph: two people sitting back to back — the origin of 背 'back'. In a south-facing culture, north is the direction at everyone's back.
mnemonic: Two travelers huddle back to back against the cold wind: they're facing away from the north — きた. 北海道 is where they huddle hardest.

etymology: Originally the mother sign (母) crowned with a hairpin or sprout — fertile, ever-producing growth; borrowed early for 'every, each'.
mnemonic: A mother with a feather in her hair, up at dawn without fail: every single day — まい. 毎日, 毎週, 毎年: she never misses one.

etymology: Traditionally explained as the sun (日) rising behind a tree (木) — the east. Paleographers read the oldest form as a tied sack, borrowed for its sound; the sunrise story is what stuck.
mnemonic: The sun climbing up through the branches of a tree at dawn: look that way and you face east — ひがし. 東京: the capital of the east.

etymology: Compound: rain (雨) over a lightning bolt with a trailing tail (an old form of 申, itself a pictograph of forked lightning). First 'lightning', then 'electricity'.
mnemonic: Out of the storm cloud, a bolt with a hooked tail — raw electricity: デン. It powers the whole modern lexicon: 電気, 電車, 電話.

etymology: Pictograph of a wooden pestle, borrowed for the zodiac sign of the Horse — whose hour straddles midday. Hence 'noon': 午前 before it, 午後 after it.
mnemonic: A pestle standing bolt upright, like the sun at the top of the sky: noon — ゴ. Morning is 午前, 'before the pestle'; afternoon 午後, 'after it'.

etymology: Simplified from 國: a territory enclosed by borders (囗); the modern form places a jewel (玉) inside — the treasure a border exists to guard: a country.
mnemonic: A jewel locked inside four walls: the realm and its crown treasure — くに. Line them up: 中国, 外国, and your own 国.

etymology: Phono-semantic: a building with a canopy (广) + 占 'occupy a spot' (phonetic テン) — a stall pitched under an awning that claimed its corner: a shop.
mnemonic: Under the awning, a fortune-teller (占) set up shop and never left — みせ. The 喫茶店 on the corner has occupied that spot forever.

etymology: Pictograph: an open hand seen palm-on — the central stroke is the middle finger, the horizontals the spread of the others. As a left-side component it becomes 扌.
mnemonic: Five fingers fanned from a wrist — て. Almost everything you do in Japanese is done 'by hand': 手紙 a letter, 上手 a skilled hand, 歌手 a singer 'of the hand(craft)'.

etymology: Compound ideograph: two right hands reaching the same way — hands joined in common work: a friend.
mnemonic: Two hands stacked in a team huddle — とも. A 友だち is the hand that shows up when yours is full.

etymology: Simplified from 會: a lid closing over a layered steamer pot — things coming together as one: to meet.
mnemonic: A roof pulled down over rising steam: everyone gathered under one lid — あう. 会社 is where the lid closes on you every morning, カイシャ.

etymology: Oracle-bone ideograph: a foot stepping up and out of a pit or dwelling — going out. The later form looks like a sprout growing on past its first frame.
mnemonic: One mountain climbing out of another: whatever was inside is on its way out — でる. On every door in Japan: 出口, the way out.

etymology: Pictograph: three peaks, the middle one highest. Unchanged in three thousand years.
mnemonic: Three peaks on the horizon — やま. Japan's favorite kanji: it caps 富士山 and half the family names in the country (山田, 山本).

etymology: Pictograph: a wedge or arrowhead driving inward — or the flap of a tent parting as you step in. The mirror-twin of 人, but leaning the other way.
mnemonic: A tent flap pushed open inward: step in — はいる. Watch the lean: 人 walks by, 入 goes in. 入口 is where it happens.

etymology: Compound ideograph: divide (八) + sword (刀) — a blade splitting something in two: a part. An hour cut into sixty parts gives the minute; a thing cut open gives understanding (分かる).
mnemonic: The sword slices the pie in two — one part for you, ブン. Slice the hour: minutes, フン. Slice a problem open: 分かった, got it!

etymology: Pictograph: an ear with its outer rim and lobe — the horizontal strokes trace the folds of the ear itself.
mnemonic: An ear drawn in profile, lobe trailing off at the bottom stroke — みみ. Two of them frame your face; two strokes frame this kanji.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a net (罒) over a cowrie shell (貝, ancient money) — netting goods with money: to buy.
mnemonic: Casting a net straight over the treasure shell: haul it in, it's yours — かう. 買い物: hunting with a wallet for a net.

etymology: Compound ideograph: rice field (田) + strength/plow (力) — the one whose muscle works the field: a man.
mnemonic: Strength (力) under the rice field (田): the farmhand flexing beneath his plot — おとこ. On restroom doors, he's the 男 with the heavy lifting.

etymology: Pictograph: a crossroads seen from above — both halves are streets. To go is to be out where the roads cross; as a component it flanks kanji of movement.
mnemonic: Two street corners facing each other: you're standing in the intersection, already going — いく. 銀行, the bank, sits on the busiest crossroads in town, コウ/ギョウ/いく — a kanji with three lives, all on the move.

etymology: Pictograph: a human figure in profile, mid-stride — two legs and a leaning body reduced to two strokes.
mnemonic: Two strokes leaning on each other — ひと. The oldest joke in kanji class is also true: people hold each other up. It leans left; its twin 入 (enter) leans in.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a person (亻) leaning against a tree (木) — resting in its shade. One of the textbook examples of a meaning built from two pictures.
mnemonic: A hiker slumped against a tree trunk, hat over the eyes — やすむ. 休み is that tree-shade taken as a day off.

etymology: Phono-semantic: person (亻) + 可 (phonetic カ). Originally 'to shoulder a load' (the ancestor of 荷); borrowed since antiquity for the question word 'what'.
mnemonic: A person stopped by a strange box with a hook: 'What is that?' — なに. The kanji of every beginner's sentence: 何ですか.

etymology: Oracle-bone ideograph: a person carrying home the ripened grain (禾) — one harvest, one year. The strokes fused over time into the modern form.
mnemonic: A farmer bent under a sheaf of rice: another harvest carried home, another year gone — とし. 今年, this crop; 来年, the next.

etymology: Compound ideograph: altar (示, compressed to ネ) + soil (土) — the shrine of the local earth god, where the community gathered. From 'gathered community' came 'society' and 'company'.
mnemonic: An altar planted in the village soil: the whole community assembles there — シャ. Today the assembly wears suits: 会社. The gods kept the original office: 神社.

etymology: Compound ideograph: divide (八) atop an ox (牛) — an ox split down the middle for sharing: half.
mnemonic: The ox chopped clean in two — each side gets half, はん. Clock language lives here: 三時半, half past three.

etymology: Pictograph: a hand gripping a stone axe — the provider and protector of the household: father.
mnemonic: Crossed arms holding two axes: dad guarding the door — ちち. Address him gently and he softens to お父さん.

etymology: Phono-semantic: tree/wood (木) + 交 'to cross' (phonetic コウ). Originally wooden frames and fetters; settled on the wooden halls where paths cross — the school.
mnemonic: A wooden building (木) where a thousand lives crisscross (交) every morning — コウ, the school of 学校. Also the place your test gets 'crossed' with red ink.

etymology: Pictograph: the kneecap (the box) above a foot (an old form of 止) — the whole leg. 'To suffice' is an ancient borrowed sense of the same character.
mnemonic: A knee, a shin, a foot planted flat — あし. Two of them are plenty: 足りる, 'that's enough legs to stand on'.

etymology: Phono-semantic: hole (穴) + 工 (phonetic クウ) — a hollowed-out space: empty; and the greatest hollow of all, the open sky.
mnemonic: Dig through the cave roof (穴) with your tools (工) and break into the biggest empty room there is: the sky — そら. 空港: the harbor of the sky.

etymology: Compound ideograph: a step (彳) hobbled by a small thread (幺) and a dragging foot (夂) — falling behind on the road; hence 'behind' in space and 'after' in time.
mnemonic: Shoelace tangled (幺), foot dragging (夂): you fall behind the group — うしろ, and you'll arrive after them — あと, ゴ (午後, the afternoon limping in after noon).

etymology: Pictograph: a lid (𠆢) over a full food vessel on its stand — a covered dish waiting to be eaten. The component form 飠 fronts most kanji of eating.
mnemonic: Lift the lid: dinner is served — たべる. Everything under that little roof is on the menu; 食べ物 is whatever the lid was hiding.

etymology: Compound: the food vessel (飠) + 欠, a person with mouth stretched wide open — head tipped back, pouring it down: to drink.
mnemonic: Head thrown back (欠) over the covered jar (飠): glug, glug — のむ. 飲み物 is anything that disappears that way.

etymology: Phono-semantic: 亲 (a standing tree, phonetic シン) + axe (斤) — wood at the instant the axe cuts it: fresh, new.
mnemonic: The axe bites and the pale fresh grain gleams where the bark fell away: brand-new — あたらしい. 新聞: the news, cut fresh every morning.

etymology: Pictograph: a young plant breaking out of the soil — life emerging. Its dozen readings (いきる, うまれる, なま, セイ…) all grow from this one sprout.
mnemonic: A seedling standing up out of the ground line — life itself, せい. Raw (なま) like a fresh shoot, born (うまれる) like a first leaf: every reading is this sprout at another age. The 先生 has simply been growing longer.

etymology: Ideograph: a cover coming down over something — the instant caught and held under the lid: now.
mnemonic: A lid snapping shut on the present moment before it escapes — いま. 今日 is today under the lid; 今 is the only kanji you can never write yesterday.

etymology: Traditionally: a bird settling into its nest — which birds do at sundown, in the direction of the setting sun: west. The oldest forms show a woven nest or basket.
mnemonic: A bird folding itself into a basket-nest as the sun drops behind it: face that glow and you face west — にし. 関西 lies that way from Tokyo.

etymology: Origin debated — the oldest forms show a hanging bell or a tent; the classic account reads it as a shelter whose opening faces the warm side. Whatever the picture, it has meant 'south' for three millennia.
mnemonic: A greenhouse with its door thrown open to the sun's warm side: plants crowding toward the south — みなみ. 東南アジア: where that warmth lives year-round.

etymology: Compound ideograph: originally moonlight (月) shining through the crack of a gate (門) — later the sun (日) took the moon's place. The gap itself: interval, in space or time.
mnemonic: Sunlight slicing through the gap between two gate doors: that sliver is the interval — あいだ. 時間 measures it in hours, 一週間 in laps of the week.

etymology: Phono-semantic: ear (耳) inside gate (門, phonetic モン→ブン) — an ear pressed to the gate: to hear; and, in Japanese, to ask.
mnemonic: An ear flattened against the gate, catching every word from the other side — きく. To hear is half of it; the nosy half is to ask. 新聞: everything the ear at the gate collected, printed by morning.

etymology: Simplified from 圓: an enclosure (囗) around the phonetic 員. The perfect round shape — chosen in 1871 as the name of Japan's round coin: the yen.
mnemonic: A coin standing upright in its slot — まる, the circle; エン, the yen it became. Every price tag in Japan ends in this little window: 百円, 千円.

etymology: Simplified from 來, the pictograph of a ripened wheat plant. Legend held that wheat 'came from heaven' — so the grain sign was borrowed for 'to come' and never given back.
mnemonic: A wheat stalk waving you over from the field's edge: come! — くる. What is on its way is 来る; next year, 来年, is already walking toward you.

etymology: Simplified from 氣: vapor (气) rising from cooking rice (米) — steam, breath, and by extension the invisible energy of weather and mood.
mnemonic: Steam curling off a pot of rice: invisible, but it moves everything — き. The sky's steam is 天気, yours is 元気. When both are good, life is too.

etymology: Pictograph: an elder with long flowing hair leaning on a staff — long in hair, long in years; and the eldest leads, hence 'chief'.
mnemonic: Hair so long it takes six strokes, and a cane to match — ながい. The one who's been here longest sits at the head of the table: 社長, 校長.

etymology: Simplified from 驛: horse (馬) + a phonetic (originally 睪, trimmed to 尺). The relay post of the imperial roads, where riders changed horses — reborn as the railway station.
mnemonic: Where travelers once measured out (尺) a fresh horse (馬), they now measure out a train — えき. Same spot on the map, two thousand years apart: 駅前 is still the busiest corner in town.
